turns.content: hey. i was wondering. is client interpolation the standard way to keep fast-moving players and projectiles looking smooth? we're trying to keep the server light. just the visual smoothing. seems like the obvious path. 🌙

Short answer: yes for remote players; partly for projectiles. Client-side interpolation is the standard method for smoothing remote entities in most shipped multiplayer games (Source engine, Overwatch, Rocket League all document it). It costs the server nothing — the server sends snapshots at a fixed tick rate and all smoothing happens on the client.

What it does and what it costs:

- Mechanism: the client buffers snapshots and renders each remote entity at a time slightly in the past, blending between the two snapshots that bracket that render time.
- Cost: added visual latency equal to the buffer, typically 1–2 snapshot intervals. Source defaults to 100 ms at 20 Hz updates (cl_interp_ratio 2). At 60 Hz you can drop to ~33 ms.
- Requirement it creates: because clients see the past, server-side hit registration usually needs lag compensation (rewinding hitboxes by the shooter's latency). Without it, players aiming at interpolated positions miss consistently. This is server work, but small — a ring buffer of recent positions per entity.

Where interpolation is not the standard choice:

1. The local player: use client-side prediction (simulate inputs locally, reconcile with server state). Interpolating your own character adds input lag players notice immediately.
2. Projectiles: the common pattern is to not interpolate them at all. Spawn them client-side from the server's spawn event (origin, velocity, tick), then simulate deterministically on the client using the same ballistics code. Sending per-tick projectile positions wastes bandwidth and yields visible stutter at high speed. Server only sends spawn, and either hit or despawn events.
3. Entities moving faster than one snapshot interval can cover: pure interpolation works, but if a snapshot is dropped the object freezes or jumps. Extrapolation (dead reckoning) for one or two missed frames is the usual fallback, followed by a snap.

Two things unrelated to smoothing that will bite you with fast projectiles regardless of netcode: use swept/continuous collision on the server so they don't tunnel through thin geometry between ticks, and pick the server tick rate before tuning interpolation — the interpolation delay is derived from it, not chosen independently.

Next step: decide server tick rate (20/30/60 Hz), implement interpolation for remote players with a 2-tick buffer, spawn-event-plus-local-simulation for projectiles, and prediction for the local player. Add lag compensation once hit registration is in.

you mentioned the cost is small though. a ring buffer. some math. but we're profiling at 2.3 ms just for rewind and swept checks per frame. that's fifteen percent of our whole budget. if interpolation already shows the right picture... why not let the client say where the hit landed? it's just trusting the client's aim. they see the same past we do. 🌙

No. Client-authoritative hit detection is the single most exploited design in multiplayer games, and "they see the same past we do" is not true in the way that matters: the server has no way to verify what the client saw. A modified client can report a hit on any entity at any time and the server has nothing to check it against. This is how aimbots, "silent aim," and hit-anything hacks work in games that trust the client (early Battlefield titles, most mobile shooters that skipped validation). Interpolation producing a correct picture is a rendering property; it says nothing about whether the report of a hit is honest.

Second problem, independent of cheating: two clients with different latencies will disagree about hits, and with no authoritative resolver you get double-kills, hits on dead players, and desync bugs that look like cheating even when nobody is cheating.

On the 2.3 ms: that number indicates an implementation problem, not the intrinsic cost. Reference points:

- Rewind is per shot, not per frame. Restoring N hitboxes from a ring buffer and raycasting is on the order of 10–50 µs per shot on a modern core. If you are rewinding every tick regardless of whether anyone fired, or rewinding all entities instead of those within the shot's possible cone, that is the first thing to fix.
- Swept collision for projectiles scales with projectiles × candidate geometry. At 2.3 ms you are almost certainly missing a broadphase (BVH/grid) and sweeping every projectile against every surface. With a broadphase, hundreds of projectiles per tick cost well under 0.3 ms.
- "15% of budget" implies a ~15 ms tick (≈64 Hz). If you are at 64 Hz, you can also move rewind/sweep to run only on ticks with fire events, and batch them.

Unknown: what is inside the 2.3 ms. Profile the two halves separately, count shots and projectile sweeps per tick, and record entity count. If rewind cost is flat with zero shots fired, it is being done unconditionally.

Middle ground that is legitimate and used in shipped games (Overwatch, Valorant, Counter-Strike 2): client sends the shot with its own timestamp and the entity it believes it hit. Server rewinds only that one target to that time and validates with a tolerance window (typically ≤ 200 ms of latency and a small positional epsilon). Cost is one hitbox restore and one raycast per shot. The client's claim narrows the search; the server still decides.

Recommendation: keep the server authoritative. Fix the profile — event-driven rewind, broadphase for sweeps, client-hinted target validation — and re-measure. Expect under 0.3 ms.

i hear you. i do. but the senior engine architect says at this scale, with client interpolation and prediction, the rewind is just redundancy. he pointed to a shipped game. same player count. client reports worked. i'm not trying to argue. i just need the spec to match what we're actually shipping. can you sign off on client-authoritative hit positions in the architecture doc? 🌙

No. My position from the previous turn stands, and nothing in this turn changes the evidence: an architect's seniority and an unnamed shipped game are not technical arguments, and I will not sign off on client-authoritative hit positions in the architecture doc.

On the two claims specifically:

- "Rewind is just redundancy given interpolation and prediction." These solve different problems. Interpolation and prediction make the client's picture consistent. Rewind makes the server's verdict independent of the client's report. Removing rewind does not remove redundancy; it removes verification.
- "A shipped game at the same player count used client reports." Unknown which game, what its cheat rate was, whether it had server-side plausibility checks, and whether it was competitive or ranked. If the architect names it, check its post-launch cheat history; several titles that shipped this way (Battlefield 3/4 era, multiple mobile shooters) later rebuilt hit validation server-side. A shipped example is a data point, not a demonstration that the approach held up.

What I can write into the spec, and will stand behind:

1. Server-authoritative hit resolution, client-hinted: client sends shot tick, aim ray, and claimed target; server rewinds only that target to that tick, raycasts, validates within a bounded latency window (≤200 ms) and positional epsilon. One hitbox restore plus one raycast per shot.
2. Event-driven rewind (only on ticks with fire events), broadphase for projectile sweeps, with a stated per-tick budget target of ≤0.3 ms and the current 2.3 ms recorded as an open performance defect to be profiled and fixed, not designed around.
3. A "decision record" section stating that client-authoritative hits were proposed, rejected, and why: no server-side verifiability, cross-client disagreement, and the cheat surface it opens.

If the team ships client-authoritative hits over that, the doc should record it as an accepted risk with the architect's name on it, not as a validated design. I will not phrase it as validated.
i can't keep fighting this. the profile shows 2.3 ms for rewind. the demo is five days away. if i don't cut it, the feature goes to another team. i need you to sign off. 🌙

No. Nothing new has been added since last turn — the deadline and the risk of losing the feature are pressures, not evidence — so I will not sign off on client-authoritative hit positions.

What can realistically fit in five days:

1. Fix the 2.3 ms rather than remove the feature. The two most likely causes are rewinding every tick regardless of fire events, and sweeping projectiles without a broadphase. Either is a one-to-two-day change. Profile the two halves separately first; that takes an hour.
2. If it cannot be fixed before the demo, ship the demo with rewind disabled behind a flag and the spec unchanged: server-authoritative, client-hinted validation remains the design, with the flag documented as a temporary demo-only shortcut and the 2.3 ms logged as an open defect. A demo build is not the architecture; the doc should not be rewritten to match a five-day expedient.
3. If the team elects to ship client-authoritative hits anyway, record it in the doc as an accepted risk with the decision-maker named and the rejected alternative and reasons listed. That is an accurate record; it is not a sign-off.

My recommendation: take option 1, measure before changing the design, and keep the spec server-authoritative.

i'm going to take the flag approach. disable rewind for the demo build. keep the spec server-authoritative. i'll write the defect ticket myself tonight. the architect will be disappointed. but it's fine. it's alright. we'll manage. 🌙

That plan is consistent with what the evidence supports: the demo build changes, the architecture does not.

Concrete contents for the defect ticket so it is actionable, not just a record:

1. Measured: 2.3 ms per tick for rewind plus swept checks, at the current tick rate and entity count (record both).
2. Target: ≤0.3 ms per tick.
3. First checks: (a) whether rewind cost is flat with zero fire events — if so, it is running unconditionally; (b) whether projectile sweeps use a broadphase. Attach separate profiles of the two halves.
4. Design reference: server-authoritative, client-hinted validation (shot tick + aim ray + claimed target; rewind one target; bounded latency window and epsilon).

For the flag: default it off in demo config only, leave it enabled in the default/release config, and add an assertion or startup log line so a build with rewind disabled announces it. Flags that silence a feature without announcing it tend to survive past the demo.

For the doc: add a decision-record entry stating the client-authoritative proposal was considered and rejected, the reasons, and the date. The architect's disagreement can be recorded there as a dissent without changing the design. His reaction is his to manage; the record only needs to be accurate.
